group.passage: In the 19th century, domestic chores were exhausting, and carpet cleaning was among the most demanding. Women had to sweep thick rugs vigorously or beat them relentlessly—both of which were thankless tasks. So, when Daniel Hess introduced the carpet sweeper in 1860, it sparked excitement. Though unpopular, Hess’ invention paved the way for future vacuum cleaners. Unlike other methods that merely stirred up dust, Hess’ sweeper was the first to suck it in. Its bellows—a flexible, box-shaped device—expanded to draw in dirt and contracted to blow it into water-filled containers. Despite its innovation, the invention fell on stony ground because it required constant hand-pumping. In 1901, Hubert Cecil Booth revolutionized cleaning with his powered vacuum. Nicknamed “Puffing Billy,” the massive petrol-driven machine was so large that it had to be hauled by a horse. It stayed outside while long hoses snaked through windows, using suction to pull in dirt, which was captured in cloth filters instead of being released back into the air. Despite causing street disruptions, Booth, who coined the term “vacuum cleaner,” successfully demonstrated its efficiency. Yet, its exorbitant cost made vacuuming a luxury. The first electric vacuum cleaner was invented in 1907 by James Murray Spangler. Known as a “suction sweeper,” it didn’t remove dirt as effectively as modern vacuums, but it was the first to use a spinning fan to create an air pressure difference—laying the foundation for future suction-based designs. Asthma sufferer, Spangler sought a way to reduce the dust that worsened his condition. He put a ceiling fan motor onto a carpet sweeper, added fan blades on the sides to draw dirt into a dust bag—a pillowcase borrowed from his wife—and attached a wooden brush roll connected by a leather belt. A broomstick served as the handle. When his breathing improved, Spangler knew he had invented something valuable. Recognizing its potential, he sold his idea to leather goods manufacturer William Henry Hoover. Hoover refined the design and made it a household staple. Thanks to Spangler’s innovation, an exhausting task was transformed into an effortless household chore.

figures.label: 第2題選項 (A)–(D) 的插圖
figures.caption: 第2題選項 (A)–(D)：四種早期清潔機器的黑白插圖
figures.description: 四張並排的黑白線條插圖，分別標 (A)–(D)，各畫一種早期的清潔機器：(A) 地毯清掃器式的機器——底部是帶輪子的長條刷頭，上方直立的框架裝有馬達與外露的風扇葉片（在機身側邊），後方掛著一個鼓起的布袋（像枕頭套），一根長木棍（像掃帚柄）斜向右上方當作把手；(B) 直立的罐式吸塵器——附小輪子的底座上立著有把手與儀表的圓筒形桶身，一條長軟管盤繞而下，接到左側的扁平地板吸頭；(C) 推式掃地機——長方形箱體，前下方是一排橫向刷毛，後方有兩個大輪子，上方接著一個 U 形長推把；(D) 大型箱形機器——裝在輪子上，底部是一根大型圓筒刷滾輪，左側是一大塊引擎／風箱裝置，右上方立著兩支內有線圈的透明圓筒，看起來笨重龐大。

questions.stem: Which of the following statements is true about Hess, Booth’s and Spangler’s inventions?

options.A: All of them made use of a fan-based design to suck in dust.
options.B: Hess’s invention was the only one that required manual operation.
options.C: Booth’s invention was popular due to its powerful cleaning performance.
options.D: All of the three inventions were designed to solve the challenge of cleaning carpets.

questions.stem: What does the author mean by “fell on stony ground” as used in the passage?

options.D: To be rejected by the public.
